opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what we actually mean by "intelligence" for a robot. If you build a brain that only works on one specific arm, with one specific gripper, in one specific lab, what you've really built is a very sophisticated controller. It's useful, but it's not general. Once you change the hardware, you're back to collecting data and retraining almost from scratch.

Look at how humans work. The core understanding of the world, that objects have weight, that a cup can spill, that you push a door before you pull it, doesn't depend on whether your hand is big or small, or whether you're holding a tool. The physical common sense is shared, and the body-specific part is a fairly thin layer on top. I believe a robot brain should be structured the same way. Most of the knowledge should be about the world and the task, and only a small part should be about the particular body.

There's also a very practical reason, which is data. Robot data is extremely expensive. Every embodiment on its own produces a tiny amount of data compared to what we have for language or images. If each robot form has to learn alone, none of them ever gets enough. But if one model can absorb data from arms, mobile bases, dexterous hands, even humanoids, then all of that experience adds up, and each new robot benefits from everything that came before. That's the only way I see to get scaling effects in robotics similar to what we saw with large language models.

And why "from the outset"? Because cross-embodiment isn't something you can easily patch in later. If you design your action space, your representations, and your training pipeline around a single robot, those assumptions get baked in everywhere. Retrofitting generality afterward is usually much harder than designing for it from day one. So even if early on it costs a bit of performance on any single platform, I think it's the right bet. The hardware in this field is still changing very fast, and the brain shouldn't be tied to whatever body happens to be popular this year.

r001.rationale: The response says a brain built for one robot is not general and must be retrained when hardware changes, but it does not state that one embodiment is unlikely to handle every task in the short term.

r002.rationale: The response says one model can absorb data from multiple embodiments and that new robots benefit from prior experience, but it does not clearly state that this enables rapid adaptation to a deployment embodiment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't actually know what the final body of a general-purpose robot looks like yet, and if you bet everything on one embodiment, you're betting on something the industry hasn't converged on.

Look at what happened with language. The reason large language models generalize is not that they saw a lot of one kind of text. They saw an enormous diversity of text, and the diversity itself is what forced the model to learn something abstract about language rather than memorizing surface patterns. I think the same logic applies to robots. If you train a brain on one robot, one arm, one gripper, one camera placement, the model will happily learn shortcuts that are specific to that hardware. It learns "this joint angle means this," not "the object is to my left and I need to reach for it." Those shortcuts look like intelligence in the lab and then collapse the moment anything changes.

So cross-embodiment is not really a product decision for me. It's a regularizer. When you force the same model to control a humanoid, a dual-arm tabletop setup, a wheeled base with a single manipulator, it has no choice but to separate the part of the problem that is about the world from the part that is about the body. The world part, understanding scenes, physics, task structure, what a person means when they say "clean this up," that's the thing we actually want to be general. The body part should be a thin adapter.

There's also a very practical reason. Robot data is scarce and expensive. Every lab, every company, every factory has a different robot. If your brain only accepts data from your own hardware, you're throwing away most of the data that exists in the world. Being embodiment-agnostic from day one means every new robot that comes online is a new data source rather than a new project.

And the last thing I'd say is about timing. People sometimes argue, build it for one body first, prove it, then generalize later. But architectures have inertia. If the action space, the observation encoding, the tokenization are all designed around one robot, generalizing later isn't an extension, it's a rewrite. It's much cheaper to design the abstraction early and let it be a little imperfect than to retrofit it after you've already optimized everything for a single embodiment.

r001.rationale: The response says the industry has not converged on a final robot body and argues for cross-embodiment design, but it does not state that one embodiment is unlikely to handle every task in the short term.

r002.rationale: The response advocates training across different embodiments and says the body should be a thin adapter, but it does not clearly say this enables quick adaptation to a deployment embodiment.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that a general-purpose robot brain should learn what is shared across bodies, while still understanding what each body can actually do. If you build everything around one robot, it’s easy for the model to learn habits that depend on that robot’s particular sensors, joints, or gripper. Then, when you change the hardware, you discover that some of what looked like intelligence was really specific to that setup.

Working across embodiments from the beginning pushes us to separate the task from its execution. The goal might be to pick up a cup, but a robot arm and a humanoid may need very different movements to accomplish it. You want them to share an understanding of the cup, the goal, and the consequences of their actions, while adapting the motion to their own capabilities.

That also creates the possibility of learning across platforms. Experience collected on one robot can help another, even if you can’t transfer the exact motor commands. It makes the initial problem harder, but I think that’s the right problem to solve if we want a brain that can generalize beyond a single machine.

r001.rationale: The response says different bodies have different capabilities and hardware-specific habits, but it does not state that one embodiment is unlikely to handle every task in the short term.

r002.rationale: It describes learning across platforms and transferring experience, but does not identify pretraining on data from different embodiments as the means for quick adaptation to a deployment embodiment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to separate what is shared across robots from what is specific to a particular body. The task—picking up an object, opening a drawer, helping someone—can be the same, even when the robot’s sensors, joints, and range of motion are very different.

If you build the brain around only one embodiment, it’s easy for it to learn shortcuts that depend on that particular hardware. When you move to another robot, you may discover that what looked like general intelligence was actually very specific to that setup.

Working across embodiments from the outset pushes you to learn more transferable representations: what the goal is, how the physical world behaves, and how actions change it. You still need a way to translate that understanding into actions for each body. But you want experience from one robot to help another, rather than having every new robot start from zero.

r001.rationale: The response says robots have different capabilities and that a brain built around one body may learn hardware-specific shortcuts. It does not state that one embodiment is unlikely to handle every task in the short term.

r002.rationale: The response says experience from one robot should help another, but does not identify pretraining on data from different embodiments or say that it enables quick adaptation to a deployment embodiment.
